name: Diego Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at the Old Bell, a pub on the market square that does food all day, and on Sundays we do roasts for about two hundred people. Mr Hollis owns it, his family's had it forty years. I'm in at ten, peel, prep, do the pies, then lunch and dinner on the grill and fryers. I'm the junior, so I get the jobs nobody wants, but Mr Hollis says that's how he learned too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars and I like Sundays, carving the beef, the place full of families after church. What wears me out is the Sunday roasts after a Saturday close, and the grease in my hair. I don't use any AI things, I don't trust them, I've got enough on my plate. I'm getting married to Ama next summer, and most of our two months of savings is wedding money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, a lot of fuss from big tech companies trying to sell something. I'd say it at the bar to the regulars and they'd agree. Good honest work still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be relieved, but money's still tight. The wedding's costing more than we thought, and the Old Bell's quieter midweek than it used to be. Mr Hollis cut the Tuesday lunch service in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working hard, ask Mr Hollis if I can learn the carving and the specials board. Cut back on going out so the wedding fund grows. Maybe do a few extra shifts at my cousin's café on my day off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit worried about money, which is just normal at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The quieter midweek, does that worry you for your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If the owner cuts another service, I'm the one with the least hours to lose, but the least to fall back on. Mr Hollis has always been fair to me though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ama feel about extra shifts at your cousin's café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, but don't kill yourself. Ama's a hairdresser, she works Saturdays, so we barely see each other anyway. That's the trade-off.

say: The AI fuss was **big tech** trying to sell something.
**Good honest work** still needs people, and the regulars would agree.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but the **wedding** is costing more than we planned.
The pub is quieter midweek, and the owner **cut Tuesday lunch**.
do: Ask the owner to teach me **carving** and the specials board.
**Cut back** on nights out so the wedding fund grows.
Pick up **extra shifts** at my cousin's café on days off.
feel: **Okay**, with ordinary money **worry** for my age.
S0.quote: If the owner cuts another service, I'm the one with the least hours to lose, but the least to fall back on.
fieldNote: Diego's pressures are a **costly wedding** and a quieter **pub trade**.
He trusts his **owner** personally and blames big tech for the hype.
He'd answer tight money with **more work**, not new skills.

steps.text: Learn carving and the specials board from the pub owner
Stop going out so the wedding fund grows
Work extra shifts at his cousin's café on days off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the big chains will use it to squeeze people, but family places like the Old Bell will keep doing things properly. I'd say people should support their local pub. I'd say that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mr Hollis would keep me. He'd maybe put the ordering on a computer, the card says that's the thinking stuff, but my job is pies and fryers. The chains would hurt the pub though, if they get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and keep working. I'd still marry Ama next summer, nothing changes there. I'd try to learn the grill properly so I'm worth more if the Old Bell has a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the chains. Not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mr Hollis asked you to use a computer system for ordering, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say can't you do it, Mr Hollis. If he insisted, I'd learn it, I'm not going to be awkward. But I'd want him to show me himself, not some video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other and keep buying local. Pastor Daniel would probably say the same from the front. People listen to that more than the news.

say: The **big chains** will use it to squeeze people.
Family pubs will keep doing things properly, so **support your local**.
think: The owner would likely **keep me**, since my job is pies and **fryers**.
**Cheaper chains** could still hurt the pub's trade.
do: Keep my **head down** and keep working.
Go ahead with the **wedding** next summer.
Learn the **grill** properly to be worth more.
S1.quote: Family places like the Old Bell will keep doing things properly.
fieldNote: His trust in a **family owner** shields him from worry about his own job.
He sees **chains** as the threat, not technology itself.
**Church and community** are where he'd voice his view.

steps.text: Keep working pies and fryers at the Old Bell
Learn to run the grill properly
Hold the wedding next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody puts the brakes on these tech firms. I'd pray about it, honestly. And I'd say families need to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think by 2031 a chain buys a robot that does pies and fryers and undercuts the Old Bell on price. Mr Hollis is sixty, he might just sell. AGI in 2028 doesn't touch me, but three years later the robots do. I'd be thirty-two with a wife and maybe a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about an apprenticeship as an electrician, someone's got to wire these robots in. I'd keep the wedding small, registry office and a meal at the Old Bell. We'd put off having a baby until I've got a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. I did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you did everything right. What does that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Left school, got a job, turned up every day, never asked anyone for anything. That was supposed to be enough. Nobody told me the rules would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then church. My uncle, Ama's parents, the people at St Luke's. I'd rather that than the government.

say: Nobody put the **brakes** on these tech firms.
**Families** need to stick together, and I'd **pray** about it.
think: **Robots by 2031** could do pies and fryers cheaper than the pub.
I'd be thirty-two with a **wife** and maybe a **baby**.
do: Ask my uncle about an **electrician apprenticeship**.
Keep the **wedding small**: registry office and a pub meal.
Put off having a **baby** until I have a trade.
feel: **Frightened** and **angry**, because I did everything right.
S2.quote: Left school, got a job, turned up every day, never asked anyone for anything. That was supposed to be enough.
fieldNote: He feels a **broken bargain**: hard work no longer guarantees a living.
He turns to an **apprenticeship** and family, not government help.
The robot timing hits his plans for a **first child**.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship with his uncle
Hold a small registry-office wedding instead of a big one
Lean on family and church friends if money runs short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so people should get a proper trade. I'd say it to the young lads at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, 2034 for the robots. I'd be thirty-five. Mr Hollis would have retired by then, so it's whoever buys the Old Bell. I'd want a trade under my belt before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep cooking at the Old Bell for two or three years, have the wedding as planned. Start the electrician apprenticeship evenings around 2029. By 2033, switch over fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I've got a plan. I can live with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford an apprenticeship wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily, the pay's low at first. Ama would carry us for a year or two. I wouldn't like that, but she'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the robots do electrical work too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the end, I don't know. But someone has to install the robots first, and that's a few years of work at least.

say: There's **time to prepare**, so get a proper **trade**.
I'd say so to the **young lads** at the pub.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
The owner will have **retired**, so I'd want a **trade** before then.
do: Keep cooking at the pub for **two or three years**.
feel: **Worried**, but I can live with a **plan**.
S3.quote: Someone has to install the robots first, and that's a few years of work at least.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **keep the wedding** and stage a move into a trade.
He'd accept his wife **carrying the household** for a while, reluctantly.
He's honest that robots might reach **electrical work** in the end.

steps.text: Keep cooking at the Old Bell for two or three more years
Live on his wife's wages during the low-paid apprenticeship years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's a whole career for some people, no need to panic. I'd tell the regulars to stop reading the papers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, robots in 2039, I'm forty. I'd have kids at school by then. I'd want to be settled in something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on cooking, get good at it, maybe be head cook at the Old Bell. Have the wedding, have a baby in a couple of years. Around 2034 look at the electrician thing seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A small worry at the back, about the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your children to cook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not if robots are coming. I'd want them in something with people, nursing maybe, or teaching. Something you need a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell the regulars not to panic, but you're steering your children away. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. Ten years is fine for me. It's not fine for someone starting out in 2040.

say: **Ten years** is a whole career for some, so **no panic**.
I'd tell the regulars to stop reading the **papers**.
think: Robots in **2039**, when I'll be forty with **kids at school**.
By then I'd want to be settled in something **solid**.
do: Work up to **head cook** at the pub.
Have the **wedding** and a baby within a couple of years.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a small worry about the **kids**.
S4.quote: Ten years is fine for me. It's not fine for someone starting out in 2040.
fieldNote: A decade restores his **family plans** on their original timing.
His worry moves to his **future children's** careers.
He admits the **contradiction** between calm advice and his own caution.

steps.text: Work up to head cook at the Old Bell
Marry next summer and start a family within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have a new wife and no trade by 2031. What would help is proper apprenticeships, paid, run by real tradesmen, not courses on a screen. And something to protect small family businesses like the Old Bell from the chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the pubs. A pub isn't just food, it's where a town meets. If a robot chain kills the Old Bell, the town loses more than my job.

headlineQuote: A pub isn't just food, it's where a town meets.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old junior cook** at a family-owned pub on the market square.
He's marrying a **hairdresser** next summer, and most of his **two months** saved is wedding money.
He's **traditional** and churchgoing, never uses AI and blames **big tech** and chains.
He'd answer change with **hard work**, family support and an **electrician apprenticeship**.
He ranges from **uneasy** in the mild scenarios to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him newly married with no **trade** by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with real tradesmen, and protection for **family businesses** from chains.
